# Platform settings · Supply allocation

## Supply routing and order

<a id="SupplyCostOrder"></a>

### Order by

Key `SupplyCostOrder` · Type enum · Default `priority`

Where: Platform settings › Supply allocation › Supply routing and order

Whether a supply's cost (its channel's list price with the channel's fee) affects the call order. Users always pay the catalog price times their group ratio; this setting affects only the platform's cost. With lowest cost, a supply is called earlier only when it meets both the minimum saving and the minimum success rate; supplies of similar cost keep the call order and share a tier by weight, and supplies of unknown cost come last.

Values:

- `priority` Call order first: Supplies are called in the call order of the providers page; cost does not change the order.
- `cost` Lowest cost: Supplies with a clearly lower cost that serve reliably are called ahead of the call order.

Examples:

- `priority` Requesty (cost x1.05) and the official API (x1.00) at the same priority with weights 3 and 1 take about 75% and 25% of gpt-5.1's requests.
- `cost` A relay at x0.80 takes gpt-5.1's requests from Requesty at a higher priority while it succeeds 95% of the time; when it drops below, Requesty takes them back.

See also: [Minimum saving](./supply.md#SupplyCostMinSavingPercent) · [Minimum success rate](./supply.md#SupplyCostMinSuccessPercent) · [Fee rate](./objects.md#channel-fee_rate) · [Priority](./objects.md#channel-priority)

Guide: [use/pricing_and_routing.md#which-supply-takes-a-request](../use/pricing_and_routing.md#which-supply-takes-a-request)

<a id="SupplyCostMinSavingPercent"></a>

### Minimum saving

Key `SupplyCostMinSavingPercent` · Type percent · Unit % · Range 0–99 · Default `5`

Where: Platform settings › Supply allocation › Supply routing and order

With cost first, how much cheaper a supply must be than another to take requests ahead of it, as a percentage of the dearer cost. Supplies closer than that count as the same cost and share requests by priority and weight, so a slightly cheaper supply does not take all of a model's traffic. 0 puts any supply that is cheaper by more than 0.1% ahead.

Examples:

- `5` OpenRouter (fee 5.5%) and Requesty (fee 5%) count as the same cost; a relay at x0.90 is put ahead of both.
- `0` Requesty (x1.05) is put ahead of OpenRouter (x1.055).

See also: [Order by](./supply.md#SupplyCostOrder) · [Minimum success rate](./supply.md#SupplyCostMinSuccessPercent)

Guide: [use/pricing_and_routing.md#which-supply-takes-a-request](../use/pricing_and_routing.md#which-supply-takes-a-request)

<a id="SupplyCostMinSuccessPercent"></a>

### Minimum success rate

Key `SupplyCostMinSuccessPercent` · Type percent · Unit % · Range 0–100 · Default `95`

Where: Platform settings › Supply allocation › Supply routing and order

With cost first, the success rate a supply needs over the current and the previous hour to be put ahead for its cost. A cheaper supply below it is ordered as if its cost were unknown, behind the supplies that serve well, until its rate recovers. A supply with fewer than 20 attempts in that time is not judged. 0 turns the check off. It is also the uptime over the last day a host of a Vercel AI Gateway model needs to be in the order of hosts the channel asks for, whichever cost order is set.

Examples:

- `95` A discount reseller that failed 12 of its last 100 requests stops taking requests first; the next healthy supply takes them.
- `0` The cheapest supply always leads, however often it fails; only pauses keep it out.

See also: [Order by](./supply.md#SupplyCostOrder) · [Minimum saving](./supply.md#SupplyCostMinSavingPercent) · [Custom pause rules](./gateway.md#PauseRules)

Guide: [use/pricing_and_routing.md#which-supply-takes-a-request](../use/pricing_and_routing.md#which-supply-takes-a-request)

<a id="ModelSupplyEnabled"></a>

### Route by supplies

Key `ModelSupplyEnabled` · Type bool · Default `false` · rarely changed

Where: Platform settings › Supply allocation › Supply routing and order

Requests are routed through each public model's supplies instead of the channels' model lists and model mappings. Turning it on first turns the channels' models and model mappings into supplies (only what is still missing), so every model a channel serves keeps working. While on, requests are billed by the public model, only published models are listed, the providers page orders the channels, and the call order, the order-by setting, intake rules and pause rules decide where a request goes. New installations start with it on. Turning it off goes back to the channels' model lists at once and keeps the supplies.

Examples:

- `false` Requests follow each channel's models and model mapping; the supply pages only preview what would change.
- `true` A request for claude-sonnet-4-5 goes to the supplies of that public model, ordered by priority and cost.

See also: [Order by](./supply.md#SupplyCostOrder) · [Intake rules for new upstream models](./supply.md#SupplyIntakeRules) · [Custom pause rules](./gateway.md#PauseRules)

Guide: [use/supply_routing.md](../use/supply_routing.md)

## Intake rules for new upstream models

<a id="SupplyIntakeRules"></a>

### Intake rules for new upstream models

Key `SupplyIntakeRules` · Type json · Default `empty`

Where: Platform settings › Supply allocation › Intake rules for new upstream models

What happens to a model a channel's upstream starts listing, for channels that add new upstream models on their own. It is a JSON array tried from the top, and the first rule whose conditions all hold decides; a model no rule matches waits for review. Conditions: endpoints (abilities such as chat, responses, images, any of them), vendors (vendor ids), families and patterns (globs such as claude-* or *-preview*), supplied (whether another channel already supplies it). action is enable (routes at once), pending (added switched off until an admin confirms), disable (added switched off) or skip (not added). placement is auto (last when others already supply it), policy (where the allocation policy puts it) or last. Empty uses the built-in rules; saved rules replace them as a whole, and a channel can use rules of its own.

Examples:

- `[{"name":"Previews wait","patterns":["*-preview*","*-exp*"],"action":"pending"},{"name":"Chat joins","endpoints":["chat","responses"],"action":"enable","placement":"auto"},{"name":"Rest waits","action":"pending"}]` The built-in rules: gpt-5-preview waits for review, a new chat model routes at once (behind the channels that already supply it), an image model waits for review.
- `[{"name":"Claude joins","families":["claude-*"],"action":"enable","placement":"last"},{"name":"Rest skipped","action":"skip"}]` A new Claude model routes at once after the model's other supplies; any other new model is not added and stays in the list of new upstream models.

See also: [Route by supplies](./supply.md#ModelSupplyEnabled) · [Order by](./supply.md#SupplyCostOrder)

## Session affinity

<a id="SessionAffinityEnabled"></a>

### Keep each session on one channel

Key `SessionAffinityEnabled` · Type bool · Default `true`

Where: Platform settings › Supply allocation › Session affinity

Requests of one client session go to the channel that served it first, so the upstream prompt cache keeps hitting. A session is recognised by the Claude Code session in metadata.user_id, a session header such as Codex's session_id, the OpenAI prompt_cache_key, or else the same system prompt and first user message. Claude Code, Gemini CLI and Codex account channels are always sticky, whatever this says. When off, each request is routed on its own.

See also: [Do not move a session on failure](./supply.md#SessionAffinityStrict) · [Session lifetime](./supply.md#SessionAffinityTTLSeconds) · [Add prompt cache markers](./gateway.md#ClaudePromptCachingEnabled)

<a id="SessionAffinityStrict"></a>

### Do not move a session on failure

Key `SessionAffinityStrict` · Type bool · Default `false`

Where: Platform settings › Supply allocation › Session affinity

When a session's channel fails, the caller gets the error instead of a retry on another channel. The channel is not paused for that model either (channel-wide pauses still apply). Moving loses the upstream prompt cache and the conversation state Codex keeps upstream. Errors that say the channel can no longer serve (a rejected key, an empty balance) still move the session. Leave it off to favour availability.

See also: [Keep each session on one channel](./supply.md#SessionAffinityEnabled) · [Retries](./gateway.md#RetryTimes)

<a id="SessionAffinityTTLSeconds"></a>

### Session lifetime

Key `SessionAffinityTTLSeconds` · Type int · Unit seconds · Range 0– · Default `3600`

Where: Platform settings › Supply allocation › Session affinity

How long a session stays bound to its channel after its last request; every request starts the time again. Account channels (Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Codex) always keep 1 hour. 0 uses 1 hour as well.

Examples:

- `3600` A coding session paused for 50 minutes comes back to the same channel; after 70 minutes it may land elsewhere.
- `300` Matches the upstream's 5-minute prompt cache: past that the cache is gone, so the session is free to move.

See also: [Keep each session on one channel](./supply.md#SessionAffinityEnabled)

## Policy settings

<a id="RoutingDecisionBillingEnabled"></a>

### Charge the decision call

Key `RoutingDecisionBillingEnabled` · Type bool · Default `true`

Where: Routing policy › Policy settings

Bills the decision call (the call an auto routing policy makes to its decision model to pick the target model) to the caller: the tokens it uses at the decision model's catalog price times the caller's group ratio, once per session, as a consume log of its own. There is no fixed fee to set; the decision model's price applies. When off, the decision still runs, but the platform pays for it and no consume log is written.

See also: [Own routing policies](./supply.md#UserRoutingPolicyEnabled)

<a id="UserRoutingPolicyEnabled"></a>

### Own routing policies

Key `UserRoutingPolicyEnabled` · Type bool · Default `true`

Where: Routing policy › Policy settings

Users and organizations can create routing policies of their own, called as policy/<name>. Users create personal policies under Routing policies in the workbench, organization owners and admins organization policies; an own policy overrides a platform policy of the same name for its own keys. When off, own policies are kept but no longer apply, and only platform policies resolve.

See also: [Policies per user](./supply.md#PersonalRoutingPolicyMaxCount) · [Policies per organization](./supply.md#OrganizationRoutingPolicyMaxCount)

<a id="PersonalRoutingPolicyMaxCount"></a>

### Policies per user

Key `PersonalRoutingPolicyMaxCount` · Type int · Range 0– · Default `20`

Where: Routing policy › Policy settings

How many personal routing policies one user can create. Policies a user already has are kept when the cap is lowered; only new ones are refused. 0 sets no limit.

Examples:

- `20` A user with 20 policies gets an error when creating the 21st.
- `0` Users can create as many policies as they like.

See also: [Own routing policies](./supply.md#UserRoutingPolicyEnabled) · [Policies per organization](./supply.md#OrganizationRoutingPolicyMaxCount)

<a id="OrganizationRoutingPolicyMaxCount"></a>

### Policies per organization

Key `OrganizationRoutingPolicyMaxCount` · Type int · Range 0– · Default `20`

Where: Routing policy › Policy settings

How many routing policies one organization can create. Policies it already has are kept when the cap is lowered; only new ones are refused. 0 sets no limit.

Examples:

- `20` An organization with 20 policies gets an error when creating the 21st.
- `5` Keeps organization policies few enough to review by hand.

See also: [Own routing policies](./supply.md#UserRoutingPolicyEnabled) · [Policies per user](./supply.md#PersonalRoutingPolicyMaxCount)
